text: Lesson 29 left Briarcliff's environment standing but wide open — no security rules on either subnet, no scoped access for the ops team, and nobody watching it at all. Before this goes anywhere near real traffic, four guardrails need to go in: network security groups, RBAC, a CPU alert, and a budget alert, in that order.

Each subnet gets its own NSG, and the rules on them say something different. web-nsg allows ports 80 and 443 from the internet, because customers need in. app-nsg allows port 8080 only from 10.20.1.0 slash 24 — the web subnet's own address range, not the internet. The app tier only ever trusts traffic that's already inside the web tier.

The ops team gets a Virtual Machine Contributor role assignment, but it's scoped to just this one resource group, not the whole subscription. That's the real point of RBAC scope: exactly the permissions the team needs, on exactly the resources that need them, and nothing wider than that.

An action group defines who gets notified — the ops team's email. A metric alert watches web-vm1 and fires if average CPU stays above 80% for five straight minutes. A budget alert watches spending on the whole resource group and fires at 80% of a $150 monthly budget, around $120.

Four guardrails, now in place: web-nsg open to the internet on 80 and 443, app-nsg open only to the web subnet on 8080, RBAC scoped to the resource group, a CPU alert at 80% sustained for five minutes, and a budget alert at 80% of $150 a month.

That budget alert is exactly what fires next. Lesson 31 picks up the moment it lands in the ops team's inbox, and walks through finding out which resource is actually driving the spend before anyone touches a single setting.
